This paper proposes RSCC, a large-scale, high-quality bi-temporal remote sensing change caption dataset focusing on disaster events. The dataset includes 62,315 pre/post-disaster image pairs with detailed, human-like captions, and provides extensive benchmarks for various Vision-Language Models (VLMs).

The paper received positive reviews, with three "Accept" and three "Borderline Accept". RSCC is the first dataset in bi-temporal remote sensing across a variety of disaster types. The use of VLMs and visual prompt engineering for annotation is a novel and effective approach to creating large-scale, high-quality data. The paper provides a reliable benchmark by evaluating multiple SOTA VLMs. Some concerns were raised about the reliance on a closed-source model and the small initial human verification rate. Reviewers suggested expanding the evaluation with LLM-based metrics, more baseline tasks (like change detection), and OOD (Out-of-Distribution) scenarios.

The authors' rebuttal was highly effective and addressed all major concerns. They increased the human verification rate, added OOD case studies, and committed to including LLM-based metrics and more detailed training information. The AC suggests that the authors carefully consider the reviewers' feedback and incorporate the comments from the rebuttal and discussion phases into the final version. Overall, the paper is recommended for acceptance.

author_final_remarks.value:
Dear Program Chairs, Senior Area Chairs, Area Chairs, and Reviewers,

We thank you for the thoughtful reviews and rebuttal discussions. Our revisions reinforce the paper’s core contributions:

(i) a first-of-its-kind bi-temporal change-captioning dataset.

(ii) a reproducible pipeline with transparent post-correction.

(iii) rigorous textual-similarity evaluation.

(iv) contributions to temporal vision–language modeling for remote sensing and pave the way towards AGI.

The feedback helped us harden these contributions without changing the paper’s scope.

Below is a concise summary of what we changed and how each concern was addressed.

Reviewer 7ZA9 — QC & transparency

• Clarified the post-correction pipeline (metadata alignment → regenerate-caption) and its role in ensuring semantic coherence.

• Expanded human verification beyond the initial 2%: additionally audited a random 10% subset; automated post-correction brought all flagged items into spec.

Reviewer a98Y — Generality & metrics

• Added OOD case studies: urban expansion (QFabric) and seasonal change (SSL4EO-S12); our RSCC-tuned model substantially outperforms a naïve baseline on both.

• Added LLM-as-judge evaluation across multiple VLMs with prompting ablations (zero-shot vs textual vs visual prompts).

Reviewer 8mqq — UHR, geography, hallucination risk

• Explained why we standardized 512×512 for v1 (cost, registration, fidelity trade-offs) and positioned UHR bi-temporal expansion as future community work.

• Validated post-correction with LLM-as-judge, showing negligible semantic drift.

Reviewer xNb8 — Detection/classification & visual prompts

• Reported change-detection and multi-label damage baselines: general VLMs are far below specialized models; our RSCCM improves but we recommend specialized models for these visual-centric tasks.

• Added a mask-grounded case study on the EBD subset and expanded human-preference evaluation to 300 samples (98% IAA).

Reviewer CghA — East Asia coverage & correction semantics

• Committed RSCC v1.1/v2 to include East-Asia events plus ongoing typhoon/flood/landslide additions.

• Clarified that we regenerate captions under corrected metadata (not word-swap).

Reviewer LH2M — Metrics, reproducibility, sensitive info

• Complemented ST5-SCS and human preference with LLM-as-judge; added training details (epochs, LR, GPUs) and clarified anonymized 512×512 crops (no precise geolocation).

Thank you for your consideration.

— Authors

Dear Reviewer CghA,

Thank you again for your continued engagement and for raising these important points. Below, we offer clarifications and revisions in response to your latest comments.

For W1, we completely agree that East Asia is a crucial region for both population density and technological infrastructure. Our initial RSCC release was built upon the xBD and EBD collections from the `Maxar Open Data Program`—which, unfortunately, do not include any events in mainland East Asia. Thankfully, we have now identified several relevant activations from `Maxar Open Data Program` and are actively integrating them into RSCC v1.1:

- Super Typhoon Mangkhut – September 14, 2018 (northern Luzon, Philippines) 
- Typhoon Vamco – November 12, 2020 (Manila region, Philippines) 
- Typhoon Goni – November 02, 2020 (Catanduanes & Bicol, Philippines) 
- Tropical Storm Megi – April 10, 2022 (Leyte & Samar, Philippines) 

Besides, we also notice typhoons, flooding and landside in East Asia (e.g. Japan, China, South Koren, etc.) during Q3 2025. We are actively gathering data from `Google Earth` and  integrating them into RSCC v2.

For W2, I aplogize for the misclarification. In our post-correction pipeline, we actually use the technique that 'prompting the model to regenerate the change caption' base on Qwen2.5-Max model. See Section 2.5 as below:

> First, the Qwen2.5-Max [54] systematically enforces metadata alignment by correcting 97 discrepancies in disaster type (e.g., resolving mismatches between "hurricane" and metadata-specified 98 "flooding") and damage descriptions (e.g., revising "minor damage" to "destroyed" based on building 99 annotations).

**The experiments actually focus on the core prompt generation instead of post-corection. We place it here to denote with textual prompt/visual prompt, our results are faithful enough, where post-correction process is a mild guarantee strategy.** The experiment we show denote an additional metric to evaluate the robustness of our captions through the whole pipeline. To be sp ecific, we additionally evalute the metric so-called LLM-AS-JUDGE using Qwen3-235B-Thinking model where 1) For each pair, we generated two captions—one with mask‑guided prompts (visual + textual mask input, as per Sections 2.2–2.3) and one without any mask information (baseline). 2) Qwen3‑235B-Thinking scored each caption on a 0–1 scale for factual completeness and relevance.

rebuttal.value:
Dear Reviewer LH2M,

Thank you for your detailed and constructive comments. Please see our responses below:

● W1: Evaluation Metrics & Building Damage Mask Guidance

In Section 6 (“Limitations”) we acknowledge that standard image–to‑text metrics (e.g., FLEUR, SPARC, G‑VEval) are designed for single‑image captioning and thus cannot fully capture multi‑image semantics. To address this, in Section 4.1 we adopt ST5‑SCS (Sentence‑T5 XXL with Sharpened Cosine Similarity) for robust contextual similarity, and in Section 4.3 we conduct human preference studies to validate model rankings. Moreover, by integrating expert‑annotated building damage masks via both textual and visual prompts (Sections 2.2–2.3), we ground caption generation in factual metadata, enhancing fidelity beyond n‑gram overlap.
To directly quantify the impact of integrating expert‑annotated building damage masks on 	caption semantic fidelity, we conducted an LLM‑as‑judge study using Qwen3‑235B on RSCC subset image pairs:

  - Setup: For each pair, we generated two captions—one with mask‑guided prompts (visual + textual mask input, as per Sections 2.2–2.3) and one without any mask information (baseline).
  - Evaluation: Qwen3‑235B scored each caption on a 0–1 scale for factual completeness and relevance.
  - Results:

summary.value:
This paper introduces a novel large-scale vision-language benchmark dataset for image change captioning on bi-temporal remote sensing imagery, addressing the lack of large-scale textual annotation datasets for this task. The key contributions are as follows:
1.	Comprehensive Annotation Pipeline: A systematic dataset annotation and curation framework is proposed to ensure high-quality textual descriptions of temporal changes.
2.	Context-Based Similarity Metric: A novel context-aware evaluation metric (Sentence-T5 Cosine Similarity) is introduced to enhance the reliability of textual similarity assessments.
3.	Benchmark Evaluation: Extensive experiments are conducted using a wide range of open-source vision-language models (VLMs) for the remote sensing change captioning task, establishing a robust benchmark for future research.

strengths_contributions.value:
This paper introduces RSCC, a high-quality benchmark dataset for disaster-aware bi-temporal remote sensing image understanding. RSCC features a large data scale, diverse disaster categories, and rich textual descriptions, facilitating the comprehension of disaster imagery by vision-language models (VLMs).

The paper introduces an innovative data generation workflow that utilizes a multimodal reasoning model, structured prompt engineering, and a robust verification mechanism. This approach ensures high quality while enabling large-scale production.

A VLM specifically trained on RSCC outperforms many general-purpose models with comparable or even larger parameter counts, demonstrating the significance and robustness of the dataset for enhancing a model's understanding of bi-temporal disaster imagery.
The presentation quality of this paper is high. Its overall structure is clear along with informative figures and tables that are easy to comprehend.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
The annotation generation process for the RSCC dataset relies on the closed-source model Qwen QvQ-Max. Although the authors ensure quality through post-correction and partial human verification, the core content generation depends on a model that cannot be publicly scrutinized, which compromises the transparency of the entire dataset construction workflow to some extent.

Only about 2% of the samples in RSCC were manually validated by three experts. Although the validation results on this subset are strong, this does not fully guarantee that the remaining samples meet the same high-quality standard. The quality of the majority relies on an automated post-processing workflow.

summary.value: This paper introduces RSCC, a dataset designed for remote sensing change captioning in disaster events. It consists of over 62,000 pairs of pre-/post-disaster satellite images with human-like, detailed change descriptions, covering diverse events such as floods, earthquakes, wildfires, and more. To construct the captions, the authors propose a pipeline combining a multimodal LLM (QvQ-Max) with visual prompt engineering and human verification, producing high-fidelity bi-temporal descriptions. The dataset is further used to train and benchmark temporal vision-language models (VLMs), with extensive evaluations across models and settings.

strengths_contributions.value:
Significant Contribution to Remote Sensing and Vision-Language Research: RSCC is a first-of-its-kind large-scale dataset for bi-temporal image captioning with a specific focus on disaster impact understanding. It fills a key gap in the field where existing datasets lack rich annotations or temporal pairs (Sec. 1, Table 1).

High-Quality Data and Annotation Pipeline: The use of QvQ-Max with structured visual prompts and building damage masks (Sec. 2.3) is innovative. The human-in-the-loop correction process ensures factual consistency, achieving 92.3% expert validation pass rate (Sec. 2.5), which is impressive for automated caption generation.

Comprehensive Benchmarking: The authors evaluate a wide range of MLLMs, including both general-purpose and remote-sensing-specific models, under various prompt settings (Sec. 4.1, Table 2). This establishes RSCC as a reliable benchmark and not just a dataset.

Better performancde：The fine-tuned RSCC model outperforms prior baselines on contextual similarity metrics (ST5-SCS 58.52%) and in human preference studies (Fig. 4), showing its utility for training robust temporal VLMs.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
Limited Coverage of Non-Disaster Temporal Events: While the dataset is well-suited for disaster scenarios, its applicability to more general bi-temporal change tasks (e.g., urban expansion, seasonal variation) is not discussed. This may limit its generalizability for broader temporal VLM applications.

Metric Choices Could Be Broader: The evaluation primarily focuses on text similarity metrics such as ROUGE, METEOR, and ST5-SCS, which are widely used but may not fully capture factual correctness, relevance, or human preference alignment in complex spatiotemporal scenes (Sec. 4.1). Although recent factual alignment metrics like G-VEval and FLEUR are briefly mentioned in the limitations, they are not applied or adapted, even though they may provide more insightful signal than surface-level n-gram matches. Furthermore, the paper could benefit from incorporating LLM-based evaluation metrics, such as VIE score or GPT-4-based rubric-based judgments, which have been shown to better correlate with human preferences in open-ended captioning and generative tasks. Including or at least discussing these approaches would provide a more comprehensive and human-aligned evaluation of model outputs.
Lack of Ablation on Prompt Engineering: While the authors highlight visual prompt design as a key contribution, more ablation analysis on how different prompt styles or input combinations affect caption quality (e.g., mask vs. no-mask, disaster type present vs. absent) would make the prompt engineering approach more reproducible and better understood.

summary.value:
This paper introduces RSCC, a large-scale dataset for disaster-aware bi-temporal remote sensing understanding, comprising 62,351 pre-/post-disaster image pairs (from 31 global events like earthquakes, floods, wildfires) paired with rich, human-like change captions. The captions are generated via a QvQ-Max MLLM pipeline, refined with metadata alignment and human verification. The dataset enables robust training/evaluation of vision-language models (MLLMs) for disaster analysis. Contributions include:
+ First large-scale disaster-focused change-caption dataset.
+ Automated captioning pipeline (QvQ-Max + metadata correction) achieving 92.3% human validation accuracy.
+ Benchmark for temporal MLLMs, showing RSCC boosts performance (e.g., 58.52% ST5-SCS vs. 45.55% for Qwen2-VL).

strengths_contributions.value:
+ First large-scale disaster-focused change-caption dataset (62,351 pre-/post-disaster pairs, 31 event types) addressing a critical gap in temporal remote sensing (Table 1).
+ Rich, human-like captions (avg. 72 words) with disaster-level annotations , surpassing prior datasets (LEVIR-CC [36], Dubai-CCD [23]) that lack temporal context.
+ Novel pipeline: Combines QvQ-Max MLLM with metadata-driven correction (98.7% disaster-type accuracy) and human verification (92.3% pass rate, κ=0.893).

limitations_weaknesses.value:
+ Static resolution: All images are fixed at 512×512 pixels (Sec. 2.1), limiting applicability to ultra-high-resolution (UHR) scenarios (e.g., XLRS-Bench [72] handles 67.5B-pixel images).
+ Geographic bias: 62% of samples are from xBD (U.S.-centric disasters) (Table 4), underrepresenting Global South regions with sparse satellite coverage. Besides, Table 4 lists 18/31 events from U.S./Europe (e.g., "Hurricane Florence"), but only 3 from Asia/Africa.
+ Hallucination risk: 7.7% of captions failed human verification (Sec. 2.5), with issues like misattributed damage levels (e.g., "minor damage" vs. metadata "destroyed").

summary.value: The authors present RSCC, a large-scale change detection caption dataset designed to support temporal remote sensing image captioning and understanding. The dataset focuses on disaster-related events, which is a timely and meaningful contribution. The authors provide extensive benchmarking results of multiple Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) for disaster response. In general, the dataset is of good quality and could be a useful resource for the community. However, there are some questions and concerns that need to be addressed.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The integration of MLLMs for disaster response is a valuable step. The paper models the disaster analysis using the remote sensing change captioning task. This focus aligns well with real-world needs in emergency management, thus quite meaningful.

2. The RSCC dataset comprises pre-/post-disaster image pairs across a variety of disaster types (floods, hurricanes, wildfires, etc.). The use of QvQ-Max for initial caption generation, followed by post-correction and human validation, is good to enhance the dataset’s quality. 

3. The inclusion of multiple MLLMs (both open-sourced and commercial) in the benchmark, with zero-shot, textual, and visual prompt configurations, provides a comprehensive performance overview. For evaluation metrics, the authors include ROUGE, METEOR, and an embedding-based similarity score (ST5-SCS), which offers a meaningful assessment than surface-level n-gram overlaps.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Regarding benchmarking
It is somewhat disappointing that the evaluation focuses solely on the change captioning task. Given the availability of building damage masks and metadata, it would be natural to also benchmark change detection (e.g., binary or semantic segmentation) and multi-label damage classification using MLLMs, comparing them to specialized change detection models in remote sensing. 

2. Regarding the visual prompt
I see that the visual prompts mentioned damage-level color encodings in addition to the two satellite images. However, it's unclear whether the change label maps are provided as part of the input to MLLMs during inference, or only the satellite images. In addition, the idea of using existing change detection models to generate input masks as visual prompts could be explored. This might offer better generalization and interpretability without relying on labeled data at inference time.

3. Regarding captioning evaluation
Evaluating free-form change captions remains inherently difficult. The reliance on (semantic) similarity to "ground-truth" captions, which are themselves automatically generated and human-refined, may introduce bias. The ground truth may not always represent the optimal caption. Incorporating human preference evaluation (as done partially in Figure 4) is a good step, but still limited.

dataset_code_comments.value: The dataset and code are accessible.

additional_feedback.value:
I would be interested in seeing the authors' rebuttal.
If my concerns are adequately addressed, I would be open to increasing my rating.

summary.value:
This paper introduces the first large-scale disaster-oriented remote sensing change captioning dataset (RSCC), addressing the current gap in datasets that lack paired time-series imagery and disaster-related semantic descriptions. It fills a critical void in the field. The experimental validation is relatively comprehensive, involving evaluations of over 10 mainstream multi-modal large language models (MLLMs).
However, the writing and figures are somewhat rough and would benefit from further refinement. Dataset constructed in this paper exhibits a geographical bias in disaster distribution. Post-Correction stage  may be overly crude.

strengths_contributions.value: This paper introduces RSCC, the first large-scale, disaster-aware bi-temporal remote sensing captioning dataset, filling a critical gap in multimodal model understanding of disaster scenarios. The annotation pipeline integrates advanced vision-language models with human verification to ensure high-quality and diverse temporal change descriptions, providing strong support for intelligent remote sensing analysis.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The dataset constructed in this paper exhibits a geographical bias in disaster distribution. Why East Asia—one of the most populous and economically significant regions—has no representation of disaster events in the dataset (Table 4).

2. In the Post-Correction stage, directly replacing mismatched words with metadata-consistent terms may be overly crude. The surrounding sentence may still carry semantics tied to the original incorrect information. How about identifying the inconsistency and prompting the model to regenerate the entire caption based on corrected metadata, ensuring semantic coherence?

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: The paper provides github links for code and dataset.

final_justification.value: The authors have partially addressed my concerns, so I keep my score. I lean toward accepting the paper, but it hasn't impressed me or struck me as particularly outstanding, so I choose a 'boardline accept'.

summary.value: This manuscript introduces a large-scale dataset (RSCC) for remote sensing change captioning, comprising 62,315 pre-/post-disaster image pairs with detailed textual annotations. The authors employ the multimodal reasoning model QvQ-Max to generate high-quality captions, train a specialized model on RSCC, and evaluate the performance of various multimodal large language models (MLLMs).

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The proposed RSCC addresses the lack of temporal image pairs and rich textual annotations in existing remote sensing datasets, covering multiple disaster types (e.g., earthquakes, floods, wildfires).
2. A comprehensive evaluation of multiple MLLMs highlights the advantages of specialized models in disaster-aware tasks.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The paper primarily relies on text similarity metrics (e.g., ROUGE, ST5-SCS), which may not fully capture the accuracy of change descriptions, especially for disaster-specific details (e.g., building damage levels).
2. While the authors use QvQ-Max for annotation and perform human verification, potential biases or errors in the annotation process (e.g., confusion between flood and hurricane damage) are not thoroughly discussed.
3. The paper mentions using NVIDIA H800 GPUs but lacks details on training time, hyperparameter tuning, or specific dependencies for code reproducibility.
4. Although the dataset is sourced from public MAXAR data, potential sensitive information (e.g., precise disaster locations) and its handling are not discussed.

title.value: RSCC: A Large-Scale Remote Sensing Change Caption Dataset for Disaster Events

TLDR.value: We introduce the Remote Sensing Change Caption (RSCC) dataset, a large-scale benchmark comprising 62,315 pre-/post-disaster image pairs with detailed change captions.

abstract.value: Remote sensing is critical for disaster monitoring, yet existing datasets lack temporal image pairs and detailed textual annotations. While single-snapshot imagery dominates current resources, it fails to capture dynamic disaster impacts  over time. To address this gap, we introduce the Remote Sensing Change Caption (RSCC) dataset, a large-scale benchmark comprising 62,351 pre-/post-disaster image pairs (spanning earthquakes, floods, wildfires, and more) paired with rich, human-like change captions. By bridging the temporal and semantic divide in remote sensing data, RSCC enables robust training and evaluation of vision-language models for disaster-aware bi-temporal understanding. Our results highlight RSCC’s ability to facilitate detailed disaster-related analysis, paving the way for more accurate, interpretable, and scalable vision-language applications in remote sensing. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Bili-Sakura/RSCC.
